edge_2164.relationship: Against 'the simplistic tropes of mixedness and hybridity that seem to fascinate so many scholars who write of Métis histories': asked 'Have not fur trade historians … already extensively documented numerous instances of Métis mixedness?', he answers that to understand the Métis 'in terms of some apparently innate mixedness is thus to reproduce the same racist depictions through which less critical commentators – among them scholars – recognize indigeneity' (2014)
edge_2164.evidence_note: His own words, 'Métis': Race, Recognition, and the Struggle for Indigenous Peoplehood (UBC Press, 2014), introduction read in the publisher's sample (pp. 3–14; pp. 3–20 rechecked 2026-10-28): p. 4, 'an overly racialized narrative that connected Métis nationhood to fur trade society'; p. 5, 'the simplistic tropes of mixedness and hybridity that seem to fascinate so many scholars who write of Métis histories', in 'a vision premised on the notion that all Indigenous peoples are mixed' (he does not deny mixedness); p. 10, 'Have not fur trade historians … already extensively documented numerous instances of Métis mixedness?'; p. 11, 'To continue to understand the Métis in terms of some apparently innate mixedness is thus to reproduce the same racist depictions'; p. 12, chapter 1 treats 'a strand of long-standing fur trade literature'. In the pages read he names no fur-trade historian, so the arrow targets the frame, not Van Kirk, Brown or Peterson. Their side in their own words: Peers and Podruchny (2010, n. 2) use 'metis' for 'all descendants of European men and Aboriginal women'; Brown, as translated there (pp. 2–3, n. 3): 'there is no single Metis core identity but rather a range along a spectrum'; Brown (2017, p. 57 n. 26) names The New Peoples and Andersen's book as the older and newer poles of the field and (pp. 57–58) offers 'of mixed descent' as a descriptive term beside 'the natives’ own categories'. Chapters 1–5 unread. Person entry, identity note and the book's source record are Agent B's. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-older-scholarship.md §§2.1–2.2) Revision 1.204: the phrase 'misrecognized as a hybrid off-shoot of two races' (p. 6) describes John Ralston Saul's 'métis civilization', not historians, and was removed from this edge (data/extension-2026/indigenous-edge-review-2026-10-28/review-B.md).

Passages used: 'to challenge the now commonplace assumption that the colonial relationship … can be reconciled via such a politics of recognition' (abstract); Taylor quoted as the influential statement (p. 28); 'Canada is no different than any other settler-colonial power' (p. 11); primitive accumulation's 'excessively temporal framing' (p. 13); 'dispossession, not proletarianization' (p. 20); Fanon 'fails to push us far enough' (p. 160). The 2014 book revises this text; quotations here are dated 2009. Wolfe is not cited in the pages read.

stage2.reason: Add Simpson's paper at the Chicago symposium 'Conditions of Settler Colonialism' (26 April 2008; programme page read) and Mohawk Interruptus p. 143 'settler sovereignty is historical (as opposed to natural)' as quoted by Barron (2017, read through a fetch tool). Not in the coordinator's stage-1 list; Barron's quotations not checked against a full text.

Add Andersen's own use of 'settler colonialism': paper title 'Mixed Ancestry or Métis? Settler Colonialism, Law and Indigenous Self-Identification in Canada's Maritimes' (Chicago symposium, April 2008; paper unread); state that the 2014 introduction speaks of 'colonial projects', not 'settler colonialism'. Not in the coordinator's stage-1 list.
Optional fairness addition: Trask 1991, p. 165 n. 1, 'Culture is not static, nor is it frozen in objectified moments in time' (read). The adjoining sentence on land stays out (OCAP item 7).

The focus quotes 'as a hybrid off-shoot of two races … rather than as an Indigenous people' as Andersen's general argument; on p. 6 the phrase describes John Ralston Saul's 'métis civilization'. Suggest adding '(of John Ralston Saul's "métis civilization", p. 6)'. Not encoded: outside the coordinator's stage-1 list.

'History-writing, she argued, "naturalises this occupation"' compresses p. 75, where the subject is 'a foreign culture that … naturalises this occupation through history-writing'. Suggested: 'the occupying culture, she argued, "naturalises this occupation through history-writing"'.
